title: Shayba ibn Uthman (ra): The Assassin the Prophet ﷺ Called Closer | The Firsts | Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
He marched in the Prophet’s ﷺ army, waiting for his chance to kill him.

Shayba ibn Uthman (ra) lost his father, his uncle and his cousins in a single day at Uhud. It is narrated that at Hunayn, when the Muslim lines broke and people fled, he found himself right behind the Prophet ﷺ with nothing between them but his sword. What happened next turned the man who came for revenge into one reported to have stood his ground beside the Prophet ﷺ. He later became a keeper of the Ka’bah, and his family holds its keys to this day.

Grief can harden into a hatred with every reason behind it. The Prophet ﷺ answered this one with a hand on the chest instead of a sword, then told Shaybah that Allah had intended better for him than he had intended for himself.

title: The Prophet ﷺ, An Angel, and An Orientation for the Ummah | Anchored Ep. 2 | Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy
description:
Manners are not the polish on top of a religion. 

In the framework Abdullah ibn Mubarak used, faith sits inside five concentric walls. Certainty at the centre, then sincerity, then the obligations, then the prophetic practices, and manners as the outermost wall of all. The order matters, because the outermost wall is the one that gets breached first. 

Lose your adab and the sunnah starts looking optional; lose the sunnah and the obligations start slipping; lose those and whatever worship is left is self-selected, which means it was never very sincere; and at the end of that sequence a person’s certainty is gone. Nobody experiences this as a collapse. It happens inward, in order, over years.

The practical edge of all this is uncomfortable, and Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy lands it hard at the end. Islam was built on five pillars, which makes those pillars infrastructure rather than decoration. Everything else is finishing work, and finishing work on a structure in shambles is not piety. It is decor.

title: False Hopes in Allah and Other Things That Won’t Help | Khutbah by Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy

There is a kind of hope in Allah that has no actions behind it, and the Qur’an gives it a name: amaniyy. False hopes. Wishful thinking. It is the counterfeit of husn al-dhann billah, thinking well of Allah, and it is convincing precisely because it wears the same face. 

Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy walks through Surah Al-Hadid verse by verse to trace four steps of this delusion: you tempted yourself, you kept delaying, you began to doubt, and your false hopes deceived you.

If you have ever told yourself Allah is the Most Merciful and then quietly stopped obeying Him, this khutbah is a very urgent reminder.

title: Aging Parents, Growing Kids and "InshaAllah Next Year" | Khutbah by Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
You may still be alive tomorrow, but this version of your life won’t be.

Your body will change. Your circumstances will change. Your children will grow older. Your parents may not always be here. The person waiting for your apology may eventually stop waiting.

So what happens to all the good we keep telling ourselves we’ll do later?

The call we keep meaning to make. The apology we keep putting off. The time we assume we’ll have with our parents and children. The charity we tell ourselves we’ll give tomorrow.
The Qur’an preserves the plea of someone who ran out of time:

“My Lord, if only You would delay me for a little while, I would give in charity and be among the righteous.” — (Surah Al-Munafiqun, Verse 10)

But the delay never comes.

This isn’t simply a warning about dying suddenly. It’s a reminder that some of the good we postpone depends on having the right person, the right moment, or the right opportunity still in front of us.

In this khutbah, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on time, aging parents, growing children, unfinished apologies, and the opportunities for goodness we assume will still be there tomorrow.

title: The One Name That Erases All Of Your Sins | Allah’s Names | Dr. Omar Suleiman | Ep. 27
description:
The end of Ramadan is a time to redouble your efforts. Support Yaqeen in these final 10 nights: http://yqn.io/c65i

What if one sentence could erase your entire record?

On Laylatul Qadr, our mother Aisha (RA) did not ask for a list. She asked one question. The Prophet (PBUH) did not give her a ladder to climb or a prayer to memorize. He gave her one name of Allah, one attribute, and one ask: O Allah, You are Al-'Afuww, the Pardoner. You love to pardon. So pardon me.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman draws a clear line between Al-Maghfirah, forgiveness, and Al-'Afuww, pardon. Forgiveness covers a sin and protects you from its consequence. Pardon removes the trace entirely, as if the sin never existed. The scholars describe it as a wind sweeping the desert floor so that not even a footprint remains. That is the level of mercy this supplication is reaching for, and it is available to anyone who asks with a sincere heart on Laylatul Qadr.

The story of Abu Bakr (RA) and his relative Mustah brings this out of theology and into real life. Mustah was someone Abu Bakr financially supported, and he was among those who slandered the Prophet's wife, Aisha (RA). When Abu Bakr found out, he cut off the support. Allah then revealed a verse asking whether Abu Bakr would not love for Allah to pardon him. Abu Bakr did not just forgive Mustah. He restored everything he had been giving him, as if nothing had ever happened. That is what Al-'Afuww looks like when it lives inside a person.

title: The Hardest Thing Allah Asks From You | Allah’s Names | Dr. Omar Suleiman | Ep. 24
description:
The end of Ramadan is a time to redouble your efforts. Support Yaqeen in these final 10 nights: http://yqn.io/c65i

What do you do when the people around you keep testing your limits?

Patience in Islam isn’t weakness. The Prophet ﷺ said that no one has ever been given a gift more vast than patience. But patience isn’t simply waiting. It shows itself in how we control anger, endure hardship, and deal with difficult people without losing our integrity.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on the Divine Names As-Saboor (The Most Patient), Al-Haleem (The Forbearing), Al-‘Aliyy (The Most High), and Al-Muta’aaly (The Supremely Exalted). Through these Names, we’re reminded that Allah’s patience with us should shape how we respond when others test us.

Patience appears in different moments of a believer’s life. Sometimes it’s resisting a temptation even when it’s within reach. Sometimes it’s enduring hardship without losing trust in Allah. And sometimes it’s remaining calm when someone’s behavior pushes you toward anger.

If you’ve ever struggled with anger or wondered how to deal with difficult people without losing yourself in the process, this reflection speaks directly to that experience. Islam doesn’t ask us to suppress emotion or ignore injustice. It teaches us how to rise above it without losing our character.

While the ummah searches for Laylatul Qadr, Masjid Al-Aqsa stands in silence. A place loved by the prophets, honored by Allah, and sacred to the hearts of believers—yet closed to those who long to pray within it.
